content:
Cost considerations:

ARUs:
Per unit cost (including SD cards)
Annual costs: batteries, refurbishment?
Storage
Data processing
Travel install/take down

Point counts:
Hourly technician
Travel
Data entry


Questions for group:

- limited on what we can do with styling. Could consider getting a CS student to help.

With cost comparison, I think we want to keep it relatively simple because everyone's project is different.  Had considered putting in there very detailed costs (e.g., hourly rate for point count tech, mileage costs, etc.), but realized that how people have to deal with those costs is very different.  Just focusing on costs that are likely to be the same across projects, and/or are new considerations for people.

ARU types: what types to include in drop-down?
Default values?
How to provide descriptions? Hover text?
Style: sidebar where you can see every option at once, or tabs that you move between?

Section,TextTag,Slide,Text,ReviewCode Welcome,w_head,3,Welcome to the Joint Venture Bird Monitoring Decision Tool!,W-1 Welcome,w_intro,3,"Designing a survey for birds can be an overwhelming task. Over the last several decades, due to an increased understanding of detection probability and advancements in analytical approaches, standards for bird monitoring have changed. Wading through the available resources and scientific papers can seem overwhelming. Further, there are many reasons to implement a survey, and the appropriate methods to use are directly related to the objectives of your organization. Our goal is to provide a set of simple questions to guide you through this process. Depending on how you answer the questions, you will end up with guidance on the best approach to take with links to resources. In some cases, you may find that existing data sources can meet your needs.",W-2 Welcome,t_NEBM,3,"The first resource that should be referenced before using this tool, is the Northeast Bird Monitoring Handbook (NBMH). Our intention is not to replace this helpful guide but to build on it. The NBMH provides a ten step process to successful bird conservation through improved monitoring, starting with establishing a clear purpose. This guide is intended to help with Steps 5 and 6: 5) Develop a statistically robust approach to sampling and data analysis and 6) Design and pilot standardized field protocols that minimize error and bias. Also visit the Bird Monitoring Toolkit by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's Land Trust Bird Conservation Initiative to walk through a set of guiding questions.",W-3 Welcome,w_ack,3,Acknowledgments: This tool was created by the Appalachian Mountain Joint Venture Monitoring Committee. Last updated July 2026., Welcome,w_citation,3,Citation: XXX. 2026. Joint Venture Bird Monitoring Decision Tool. https://elizabethahunter.github.io/amjv-monitoring-tool/ Last updated July 2026., Tool,t_geog_q,4,What is your geographic area of interest?, Tool,t_geog_desc_r,4,Regional scale geographic areas include multiple counties to multiple states.,SCL-1 Tool,t_geog_desc_l,4,"Local scale geographic areas include a single military base, wildlife management area, wildlife refuge, etc.",SCL-2 Tool,t_question_q,7,What is your question of interest? Choose from the four options below:, Tool,t_question_e,7,What are the effects of management or impact of an event?, Tool,t_question_e_ex,7,"Effects of management are best assessed at the local scale where bird response to management can be measured within close proximity to the management/disturbance event. That said, there may be interest in bird response to broad scale changes in management or to a disturbance that spans an entire region. For these instances, it is best to select the (Dynamics (trends) of a target species or community over time) button and keep in mind the time frame of the change in management or disturbance in your region of interest.",Q-1 Tool,t_question_s,7,What is the current snapshot of a species' or community's distribution?, Tool,t_question_s_ex,7,"Sometimes range maps do not show the level of detail we need in a region of interest, especially if we aim to implement conservation efforts for a focal species and need to prioritize locations for these efforts. Select this option if you are interested in having more detailed information about the current distribution of a focal species or group of species in your region. Distribution could be measured in multiple ways (e.g., presence or relative abundance).",Q-2 Tool,t_question_d,7,What are the dynamics (trends) of a target species or community over time?, Tool,t_question_d_ex,7,"One of the most important metrics to inform conservation is whether populations or communities are changing over time - this can be changes in relative abundance (i.e., population trends), changes in occupancy (i.e., sites being colonized or becoming locally extinct), or species turnover. Being able to link these changes to the effects of management, conservation actions, or the impact of natural processes is especially valuable.",Q-3 Tool,t_question_p,7,What is a target species' population size?, Tool,t_question_p_ex,7,"Population size is an estimate of the number of individual birds of a particular species in a region of interest. Note that the larger the geographic area of interest, the less precise our estimate of population size will be. However, population size estimates are often essential for determining whether a species should be considered of greatest conservation need. Consider choosing the local scale if you need a precise population size estimate.",Q-4 Tool,t_metric_q,8,What is your metric of interest? Choose from the three options below. Do you want to know:, Tool,t_metric_r,8,the number and composition of priority species in your region? (Richness), Tool,t_metric_r_ex,8,"Bird community richness or other diversity metrics for all species within a region is not easy to obtain, but is much more tractable for a list of priority species (e.g., Species of Greatest Conservation Need for a habitat).",SN-R-1 Tool,t_metric_o,8,where or in what season a target species occurs within your region? (Occupancy), Tool,t_metric_o_ex,8,"Occupancy is whether or not a species is likely present in a certain location, and is typically presented as a probability of occupancy. Within a broader region of interest, it may only be necessary to know species occupancy at coarse spatial scales (e.g., within 2km) rather than at individual sites.",SN-O-1 Tool,t_metric_a,8,which areas have higher or lower relative abundance for a target species within your region? (Relative Abundance), Tool,t_metric_a_ex,8,"Relative abundance is the relative number of individual birds of a given species for a given area. The term relative is used because we are rarely able to know the exact number of birds, and our estimated values of abundance are typically adjusted for detection probability. Relative abundance is therefore not true abundance, but it provides a valuable index that can be compared across sites and regions.",SN-A-1 Tool,t_metric_trend_q,,What is your metric of interest? Choose from the three options below. Do you want to know:, Tool,t_metric_trend_r,,change in the number and composition of species in your region (richness) over a set time interval?, Tool,t_metric_trend_r_ex,,"Tracking changes to bird community richness for all species within a region is not easy, thus we recommend focusing on a list of priority species (e.g., Species of Greatest Conservation Need for a given habitat).",TR-R-1 Tool,t_metric_trend_o,,the change in probability of occurrence of a target species over time? (Occupancy), Tool,t_metric_trend_o_ex,,"Occupancy is whether or not a species is likely present in a certain location, and is typically presented as a probability of occupancy. Within a broader region of interest, it may only be necessary to know species occupancy at coarse spatial scales (e.g., within 2km) rather than at individual sites. Trends in occupancy allow you to track whether species are colonizing new sites or going locally extinct over time.",TR-O-1 Tool,t_metric_trend_a,,how has relative abundance changed over time for a target species within your region? (Relative Abundance), Tool,t_metric_trend_a_ex,,"Relative abundance is the relative number of individual birds of a given species for a given area. The term relative is used because we are rarely able to know the exact number of birds, and our estimated values of abundance are typically adjusted for detection probability. Relative abundance is therefore not true abundance, but it provides a valuable index that can be compared across sites and regions. Choose the Population Size question at the level above if you want to estimate true abundance.",TR-A-1 EndPoint,ep_RE,,"Effects of management are best assessed at the local scale where bird response to management can be measured within close proximity to the management/disturbance event. That said, there may be interest in bird response to broad scale changes in management or to a disturbance that spans an entire region. For these instances, it is best to select 'Dynamics (trends) of a target species or community over time' and keep in mind the time frame of the change in management or disturbance in your region of interest.",EFF-1 EndPoint,ep_RSO,9,"For this type of objective, we recommend using either eBird or BBA. Below are some clarifying questions to help you decide which resource to use.",SN-O-2 EndPoint,ep_RSO_s,9,Does eBird represent your focal species well?,SN-O-3 EndPoint,ep_RSO_s_ex,9,"When considering the suitability of eBird data products for a given species, it is important to consider detection probability, i.e. whether any aspect of the species behavior results in a low likelihood of detection by an observer. This can be driven by low overall abundance within a given geography, easily mis-identified song/call types, and/or nocturnal activity patterns.",SN-O-4 EndPoint,ep_RSO_e,9,What is eBird coverage in your region?,SN-O-5 EndPoint,ep_RSO_e_ex,9,"The eBird database is populated by observations made by birders around the world. When considering using these data products, it is important to evaluate whether your target geography (or the surrounding region) is likely to be underbirded due to remoteness, accessibility challenges, or simply because it is a rural area with low human population densities.",SN-O-6 EndPoint,ep_RSO_b,9,When was the last Breeding Bird Atlas (BBA) in your region/state?,SN-O-7 EndPoint,ep_RSO_b_ex,9,"Breeding bird atlas projects (BBAs) can provide very detailed data on bird distributions at specific points in time, typically during a 5-year survey period. Consider whether the latest BBA in your target geography is close enough to your time period of interest.",SN-O-8 EndPoint,ep_RSO_local,,"If after considering these questions and looking at the resources below you do not think these tools meet your needs, you may need to collect your own data at a local scale. To explore local options, click the Reset button at the top of the page and then the Local button.",SN-O-9 EndPoint,ep_RTO,,"For this type of objective, we recommend using either eBird or BBA resources. Below are some clarifying questions to help you decide which resource to use.",TR-O-2 EndPoint,ep_RTO_s,,Does eBird represent your focal species well?,TR-O-3 EndPoint,ep_RTO_s_ex,,"When considering the suitability of eBird data products for a given species, it is important to consider detection probability, i.e. whether any aspect of the species behavior results in a low likelihood of detection by an observer. This can be driven by low overall abundance within a given geography, easily mis-identified song/call types, and/or nocturnal activity patterns.",TR-O-4 EndPoint,ep_RTO_e,,What is eBird coverage in your region?,TR-O-5 EndPoint,ep_RTO_e_ex,,"The eBird database is populated by observations made by birders around the world. When considering using these data products, it is important to evaluate whether your target geography (or the surrounding region) is likely to be underbirded due to remoteness, accessibility challenges, or simply because it is a rural area with low human population densities.",TR-O-6 EndPoint,ep_RTO_b,,When was the last Breeding Bird Atlas (BBA) in your region/state?,TR-O-7 EndPoint,ep_RTO_b_ex,,"Breeding bird atlas projects (BBAs) can provide very detailed data on bird distributions at specific points in time, typically during a 5-year survey period. Consider whether the latest BBA in your target geography is close enough to your time period of interest.",TR-O-8 EndPoint,ep_RTO_local,,"If after considering these questions and looking at the resources below you do not think these tools meet your needs, you may need to collect your own data at a local scale. To explore local options, click the Reset button at the top of the page and then the Local button.",TR-O-9 EndPoint,ep_RSR,,"eBird Status and Trends combines raw eBird data, satellite imagery, statistical models, and machine learning to predict species richness and relative abundance across space and time. For this type of objective, you will need some experience with the R programming language. We will point you to resources that provide the majority of code needed, but you will need to modify the code to suit your needs. The functions for downloading and working with eBird Status and Trend Rasters are available through the ebirdst package in R.",SN-R-2 EndPoint,ep_RSR_clarify,,"Before embarking on this, you might want to consider what eBird coverage is like in your region. This is especially true if your region is relatively small (e.g., a few, rural counties) and under-birded. The eBird Status and Trend data products may be biased in such regions. Larger regions (e.g., states) will be unbiased.",SN-R-3 EndPoint,ep_RSA,,"For this type of objective, we recommend using either eBird or estimates from the Breeding Bird Survey (BBS, used for Partners in Flight estimates). Below are some clarifying questions to help you decide which resource to use.",SN-A-2 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q1,,How many BBS routes are in your region of interest?,SN-A-3 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q1_ex,,You can see the location of BBS routes in your region at the BBS Route Map. Note: these maps may load slowly and it may be difficult to know whether they are up to date.,SN-A-4 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q2,,Does BBS or eBird represent your focal species well?,SN-A-5 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q2_ex,,"When considering the suitability of BBS or eBird data products for a given species, it is important to consider detection probability, i.e. whether any aspect of the species behavior results in a low likelihood of detection by an observer. This can be driven by low overall abundance within a given geography, easily mis-identified song/call types, and/or nocturnal activity patterns.",SN-A-6 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q3,,What is eBird coverage in your region?,SN-A-7 EndPoint,ep_RSA_q3_ex,,"The eBird database is populated by observations made by birders around the world. When considering using these data products, it is important to evaluate whether your target geography (or the surrounding region) is likely to be underbirded due to remoteness, accessibility challenges, or simply because it is a rural area with low human population densities.",SN-A-8 EndPoint,ep_RTA,,"For this type of objective, we recommend using either eBird or estimates from the Breeding Bird Survey (BBS, used for Partners in Flight estimates). Below are some clarifying questions to help you decide which resource to use.",TR-A-2 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q1,,How many BBS routes are in your region of interest?,TR-A-3 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q1_ex,,You can see the location of BBS routes in your region at the BBS Route Map. Note: these maps may load slowly and it may be difficult to know whether they are up to date.,TR-A-4 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q2,,Does BBS or eBird represent your focal species well?,TR-A-5 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q2_ex,,"When considering the suitability of BBS or eBird data products for a given species, it is important to consider detection probability, i.e. whether any aspect of the species behavior results in a low likelihood of detection by an observer. This can be driven by low overall abundance within a given geography, easily mis-identified song/call types, and/or nocturnal activity patterns.",TR-A-6 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q3,,What is eBird coverage in your region?,TR-A-7 EndPoint,ep_RTA_q3_ex,,"The eBird database is populated by observations made by birders around the world. When considering using these data products, it is important to evaluate whether your target geography (or the surrounding region) is likely to be underbirded due to remoteness, accessibility challenges, or simply because it is a rural area with low human population densities.",TR-A-8 EndPoint,ep_RTR,,"eBird Status and Trends combines raw eBird data, satellite imagery, statistical models, and machine learning to predict species richness, occurrence, and population trends across space and time. For this type of objective, you will need some experience with R. We recommend using the eBird Trend map tool OR the eBird ST package in R.

eBird Trend Map Tool (no R required):
The simplest option is the eBird Trend map tool, which provides a detailed visualization of population trajectory and short-term (10-year) trend estimates for most North American bird species at high spatial resolutions (27x27km). While this requires evaluating species individually, it is the quickest way to access trend information for any given geography. This tool also provides trend confidence intervals. See also the detailed explanation of trend maps.

eBird ST R Package:
For users comfortable with R, you can access and download trend data through the eBirdST package. The eBird Trends Data Product guidance page walks you through downloading and customizing eBird trend rasters for your target species and/or geography. For richness, stacking breeding season abundance rasters identifies areas of highest importance for a set of focal species — see the eBird ST Applications page (scroll to 'Areas of Importance') for instructions and code.",TR-R-2 EndPoint,ep_RPS,,For this type of objective we recommend using either Breeding Bird Atlases (BBAs) or estimates from the Partners In Flight (PIF) Population Estimates Database. Below are some clarifying questions to help you decide which resource to use. Note that estimates of population size at broad regional scales are potentially prone to many sources of error — good estimates will have a measure of uncertainty associated with them (e.g. confidence intervals or standard deviations) which should always be taken into account.,PS-1 EndPoint,ep_RPS_bba_q,,When was the last Breeding Bird Atlas (BBA) in your region/state?,PS-6 EndPoint,ep_RPS_bba_ex,,"Breeding bird atlas projects (BBAs) can provide very detailed data on bird distributions at specific points in time, typically during a 5-year survey period. Consider whether the latest BBA in your target geography is close enough to your time period of interest.",PS-7 EndPoint,ep_RPS_pif_q,,Does the PIF database represent your focal species well?,PS-8 EndPoint,ep_RPS_pif_ex,,The models used to populate the PIF population estimates database rely on the North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) and increasingly eBird data sources and thus are prone to the same biases as these datasets. When considering the suitability of these data products for a given species it is important to consider detection probability i.e. whether any aspect of the species behavior results in a low likelihood of detection by an observer. This can be driven by low overall abundance within a given geography easily mis-identified song/call types and/or nocturnal activity patterns.,PS-9 EndPoint,ep_RPS_local,,If after considering these questions and looking at the resources below you do not think these tools meet your needs you may need to collect your own data at a local scale. To explore local options click the Reset button at the top of the page and then the Local button.,PS-10 Resources,eBird_occ_ex,10,"eBird is a citizen science platform where birders of any skill level can submit checklists of the birds they see or hear. eBird checklists can include data such as presence, abundance, and breeding codes. These checklists are reviewed by automated filters and trained ebird moderators to flag any unusual or potentially incorrect submissions. eBird Status and Trends scientists combine raw eBird data, satellite imagery, statistical models, and machine learning to predict population trends and occurrence across space and time. These population and occurrence predictions are then built into visualizations and summary statistics designed for professional use.",SN-O-10 Resources,eBird_occ,10,"Check out eBird Status and Trends and type in your species of interest. Maps are predictions of relative abundance (occupancy can be inferred by any pixel that is colored in, and areas in gray are where the species is inferred to be absent). You can get regional estimates using drop down menus (country/state, and ultimately other regions like JVs) or drawing a polygon. The maps may provide more nuanced information than these estimates, especially if your state covers different ecoregions where trends may differ. If you have some R experience, you can follow tutorials to get encounter rate, which is proportional to occupancy. You can also download raw eBird data from GBIF. Survey Design

Number of Points: The number of survey points required depends on the level of natural variation in your system, the magnitude of change you want to be able to detect, and your acceptable risk of missing a real effect (statistical power). More variable environments — whether due to habitat heterogeneity, species rarity, or observer inconsistency — require more points to achieve the same precision. As a general rule, aim for enough points to detect a biologically meaningful change (e.g., a 20–30% decline over the monitoring period) with at least 80% power. Free tools such as G*Power and the R package pwr can help formalize power calculations, though even rough back-of-envelope estimates are better than none. Consulting a statistician or biometrician early in the planning process is strongly recommended for projects that will inform high-stakes decisions.

Number of Years: Longer monitoring windows improve the ability to detect gradual trends and separate real biological change from year-to-year environmental noise (e.g., drought years, late springs). However, longer commitments also increase total cost. Three to five years is often cited as a minimum for detecting directional trends in common species; rare species or subtle effects may require a decade or more. Consider whether your question requires a formal trend estimate or whether an occupancy change between two well-defined periods (e.g., before vs. after a management action) could be answered with a shorter, more targeted design.

ARU Type

There are a variety of ARUs available on the market to fit your budget and project needs. Typically, more expensive units have higher-quality technical specifications such as calibrated microphones, higher memory storage capacity, and extended battery life. They may also offer additional features such as multi-channel recording, external power capabilities, ultrasonic recording options, or built-in time-synced GPS. When choosing a device, consider your equipment budget, minimum number of devices needed to complete the project, user-interface preferences, and the battery and memory requirements based on how often personnel can access the ARUs. Listed below are some of the available ARUs spanning a cost spectrum from popular sellers like Open Acoustic Devices, Wildlife Acoustics, Frontier Labs, Titley Scientific, and Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

Memory Card Type

Most ARUs store memory on either SD cards or microSD cards depending on the brand and model. The cost of the memory card will increase as the storage size increases. Most ARUs have a data estimator tool within their user interface to calculate memory usage based on your recording schedule. Choose the next size up from what your storage needs require (e.g., estimated 100 GB data → 128 GB memory card). Consider your recording schedule to optimize data collection and reduce memory needs — you probably need less data than you think for most questions. Estimated cost range: $7–$250 per card depending on storage capacity.

Annual ARU Installation Costs

When estimating the costs of installing and recovering ARUs, consider the following:

Field technicians:

  • Hourly rate (e.g., $15)
  • Hours per week (e.g., 40) — include travel time, site access, ARU set-up, and data entry/upload
  • Number of weeks (e.g., 12) — consider the phenology of the focal species, spatial distribution of the project, and deployment duration
  • For the example numbers above, that comes to $7,200/technician, not including any fringe benefits

Transportation:

  • Rental car and gas
  • Mileage if technicians use their own vehicles

Lodging:

  • Options include rental houses, camping, hotels, and hostels — costs vary widely. The best option depends on how broad a region you need to cover, the climate, and comfort levels.

Other considerations:

  • Any ancillary data collected at ARU locations (e.g., habitat surveys) — factor in the time required
  • Number of visits to each ARU
  • Time for prepping ARUs: updating firmware, configuring SD cards, loading recording schedules, installing batteries, testing and calibrating equipment

Annual Supplies Costs

Include in your budget common yearly purchases necessary to run ARUs.

Batteries and memory: Unless your unit has an external solar power source or rechargeable batteries, expect to purchase batteries at least yearly. Replacement SD cards may be needed as some lose functionality over repeated use. Estimated cost range: $100–$1,000 per year.

Security and housing: Depending on your ARU and security needs, zip ties, screws, anti-static bags, cable locks, padlocks, plastic or steel cases, or desiccant packets may need to be purchased annually or replaced occasionally. Estimated cost range: $50–$500 per year.

Repairs: ARUs can become damaged during deployment from people, wildlife, or the elements. Budget for common, less expensive repairs (replacement wind screens, gaskets, or power/microphone cables) and rarer, more expensive repairs (microphone replacements, ARU chip repairs, or whole ARU replacements). A conservative estimate is to budget 10% of initial ARU costs for annual replacement costs.

Annual Data Processing Costs

After acquiring recordings, it is typically not feasible to listen to them all manually. Multiple freely available automatic processing options exist. Classifiers such as Kaleidoscope and Arbimon require training a model using known recordings of a species — most useful when focusing on one or a few species. Pre-trained whole-community models such as BirdNet-Analyzer may be less accurate for individual species but allow for broader community identification.

If deploying only a few ARUs for a single season, using online or desktop applications is feasible and a technician could process data in a couple of weeks. For larger projects, contracting with a data specialist who can process large amounts of data is likely more time-effective. Estimated cost range: $500–$5,000 per year.

Storage Costs

Long-term data storage needs vary in price depending on the amount of data stored annually. Explore the options below to find the best combination for your project. We strongly recommend storing data redundantly in at least two places.

External hard drives: Helpful for active data processing, small projects, or sharing data between partners. However, they can fail unexpectedly, especially as drives age. Use as a secondary or backup storage method, or back up data across multiple hard drives. Estimated cost: $100–$300 per portable drive; $200–$800 per desktop drive. Typical storage: up to ~5 TB portable, up to ~25 TB desktop.

Network Attached Storage (NAS): A NAS is a dedicated file-storage appliance with multiple drives that automatically copies data across drives, protecting against individual drive failure. Also accessible by multiple approved users over a network. Estimated cost: $1,000–$6,000 per NAS. Typical storage: ~64–120 TB desktop; up to ~200 TB for high-end options.

Cloud-based storage: Cloud storage hosts data on remote servers accessible via the internet, with varying degrees of multi-user access, scalability, redundancy, and privacy. May be appealing if integrated into your workplace ecosystem (e.g., Google Drive, OneDrive). Some providers offer long-term “cold” storage at lower rates for archived data. Estimated cost: $1–$100 per month depending on storage needs.

Public data archives: If data privacy is not a restriction, data can be stored on public archives, some of which offer version control. Examples include Zenodo, Open Science Framework, Dataverse, Figshare, and Archive.org. Estimated cost: free.

All-in-one platforms: Pipelines are emerging that support acoustics research from start to finish. Arbimon offers unlimited free storage for audio files under 200 MB and provides support from research question development through data analysis and visualization. Ecosounds also offers free storage and prefers files ranging from 1 hour to 1 day in duration. Please review each platform’s terms of service, privacy policies, and data sharing policies before committing, and explore their analysis tools to determine if they suit your research questions. Estimated cost: varies by scale.

Annual Point Count Costs

When estimating the costs of conducting point count surveys, consider the following:

Field technicians:

  • Hourly rate (e.g., $15)
  • Hours per week (e.g., 40) — include travel time and data entry
  • Number of weeks (e.g., 12) — consider the breeding phenology of any focal species in your region and allow a few days of training at the start of the season
  • For the example numbers above, that comes to $7,200/technician, not including any fringe benefits

Transportation:

  • Rental car and gas
  • Mileage if technicians use their own vehicles

Lodging:

  • Options include rental houses, camping, hotels, and hostels — costs vary widely. The best option depends on how broad a region you need to cover, the climate, and comfort levels.

Supplies:

  • Binoculars ($200–$500)
  • Rangefinders for distance estimation ($40–$400)
  • Printed datasheets
  • Clipboards ($10–$40)

Other considerations:

  • Any ancillary data to be collected at point count locations — factor in the time required
  • Number and spatial distribution of points
  • Number of visits to each point

Data collected over multiple visits within a season or by multiple simultaneous observers can also be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about point count surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-SO-T-PC EndPoint,pc_LSA,,"Point Counts: An observer stands at a fixed location for a set period (typically 3-10 minutes) and records all birds detected by sight or sound. For a snapshot of relative abundance deploy points using a systematic random or stratified random design across representative habitat on your site. Relative abundance can be compared across habitat types and related to habitat features. To account for imperfect detection, observed birds are often assigned to distance bands and/or the minute in which they are observed. Data collected over multiple visits within a season or by multiple simultaneous observers can also be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about point count surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-SA-T-PC EndPoint,pc_LTR,,"Point Counts: An observer stands at a fixed location for a set period (typically 3-10 minutes) and records all birds detected by sight or sound. For trends in richness return to the exact same locations each year during the same part of the breeding season. Fixed locations revisited repeatedly allow changes in community composition to be attributed to real biological change rather than sampling variation. The number of observed species (richness) can be tracked over time at each point. To account for imperfect detection, observed birds are often assigned to distance bands and/or the minute in which they are observed. Data collected over multiple visits within a season or by multiple simultaneous observers can also be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about point count surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-TR-T-PC EndPoint,pc_LTO,,"Point Counts: An observer stands at a fixed location for a set period (typically 3-10 minutes) and records all birds detected by sight or sound. For occupancy trends return to the same fixed locations each year with multiple visits per season to estimate detection probability. Consistent timing and effort across years is critical for detecting real changes in occupancy. To account for imperfect detection, observed birds are often assigned to distance bands and/or the minute in which they are observed. Data collected over multiple visits within a season or by multiple simultaneous observers can also be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about point count surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-TO-T-PC EndPoint,pc_LTA,,"Point Counts: An observer stands at a fixed location for a set period (typically 3-10 minutes) and records all birds detected by sight or sound. For trends in relative abundance return to the same fixed locations each year during the same period. Identical locations and consistent effort across years ensures changes in counts reflect actual changes in abundance rather than sampling variation. To account for imperfect detection, observed birds are often assigned to distance bands and/or the minute in which they are observed. Data collected over multiple visits within a season or by multiple simultaneous observers can also be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about point count surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-TA-T-PC EndPoint,trans_LER,,"Transect Surveys: An observer walks a set path and records all birds seen or heard within a fixed-width distance band. For effects of management place transects to cross management boundaries or replicate them across management treatments and control areas. The number of observed species (richness) can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected along transect routes. Data collected over multiple visits within a season, by multiple simultaneous observers, or using information from distance bands can be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about transect surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-ER-T-TR EndPoint,trans_LEO,,"Transect Surveys: An observer walks a set path and records all birds seen or heard within a fixed-width distance band. For effects of management on occupancy place transects to cross management boundaries or replicate them across management treatments and control areas. Occupancy can be estimated as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected along transect routes. Data collected over multiple visits within a season, by multiple simultaneous observers, or using information from distance bands can be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about transect surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-EO-T-TR EndPoint,trans_LEA,,"Transect Surveys: An observer walks a set path and records all birds seen or heard within a fixed-width distance band. For effects of management on relative abundance place transects to cross management boundaries or replicate them across management treatments and control areas. Relative abundance can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected along transect routes. Data collected over multiple visits within a season, by multiple simultaneous observers, or using information from distance bands can be used to account for imperfect detection. You can learn more about transect surveys here and see example protocols here.",L-EA-T-TR EndPoint,trans_LSR,,"Transect Surveys: An observer walks a set path and records all birds seen or heard within a fixed-width distance band. See the Cornell Bird Monitoring Toolkit for protocols.",L-SA-T-FL EndPoint,fixed_LTR,,"Fixed Location Counts: An observer returns to the same vantage point each year and records all birds within view or earshot during a set time period. This approach works well for waterbirds, migrating raptors, colonial nesters, and other species detectable from a distance, and is especially powerful for tracking richness trends because the identical area is surveyed consistently across years. See the Cornell Bird Monitoring Toolkit for protocols.",L-TR-T-FL EndPoint,fixed_LTO,,"Fixed Location Counts: An observer returns to the same vantage point each year and records all birds within view or earshot during a set time period. This approach works well for waterbirds, migrating raptors, colonial nesters, and other species detectable from a distance. For occupancy trends the fixed location ensures that changes in detection reflect real changes in species presence. Visit each point at least twice per season to estimate detection probability. See the Cornell Bird Monitoring Toolkit for protocols.",L-TO-T-FL EndPoint,fixed_LTA,,"Fixed Location Counts: An observer returns to the same vantage point each year and records all birds within view or earshot during a set time period. This approach works well for waterbirds, migrating raptors, colonial nesters, and other species detectable from a distance. For trends in relative abundance revisiting the exact same location each year controls for spatial variation ensuring count changes reflect real abundance trends. See the Cornell Bird Monitoring Toolkit for protocols.",L-TA-T-FL EndPoint,aru_LER,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. The number of species (richness) can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected at the deployment points. For effects of management on richness deploy ARUs across management categories or along a management gradient with control locations. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-ER-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LEO,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Occupancy can be estimated as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected at the deployment points. For effects of management on occupancy deploy ARUs across management treatments and control areas. Multiple recording sessions per season allow occupancy estimation accounting for imperfect detection. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-EO-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LEA,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Relative abundance can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected at the deployment points. For effects of management on relative abundance deploy ARUs across management categories or along a management gradient with control areas. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-EA-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LSR,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. For a snapshot of richness deploy ARUs using a systematic random or stratified random design across your site. ARUs are particularly useful for detecting secretive and nocturnal species missed by daytime point counts. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SR-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LSO,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. For occupancy estimation use a systematic random or stratified random design and collect multiple recording sessions per season at each location to estimate detection probability. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SO-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LSA,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. For a snapshot of relative abundance deploy ARUs using a systematic random or stratified random design across representative habitats on your site. Acoustic detection rates from automated classifiers provide an index of relative abundance. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SA-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LTR,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. For trends in richness return ARUs to the exact same locations each year during the same period. Consistent deployment timing and duration across years ensures changes in detected richness reflect real biological change. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TR-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LTO,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. For occupancy trends return ARUs to the same fixed locations each year with consistent deployment periods. Multiple recording sessions per season allow occupancy estimation accounting for detection probability. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TO-T-AR EndPoint,aru_LTA,,"Acoustic Monitoring: Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) are passive recorders deployed at fixed locations that capture bird vocalizations continuously or on a schedule. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. For trends in relative abundance return ARUs to the same fixed locations each year during the same period. Acoustic detection rates from automated classifiers provide an index of relative abundance. Consistent deployment ensures that changes in acoustic detection rates reflect real changes in abundance. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. You can learn more about acoustics here, see example protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TA-T-AR EndPoint,ebird_LER,,"eBird: eBird is a citizen science platform where observers submit bird checklists. For effects-of-management questions eBird data are primarily observational and cannot replace controlled surveys with treatment and control areas. However checklists from your site can provide a useful baseline species list and supplement structured surveys. Note that observer effort and coverage may be uneven across your site. Treat eBird data for effects questions with appropriate caution and consider pairing with structured surveys. Search for observations from your site on eBird Explore. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, additional tools and resources here, and see how eBird can be used for effects monitoring here.",L-ER-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LEO,,"eBird: eBird checklists from your site can indicate whether a species has been detected and provide presence/absence data across seasons. For occupancy estimation from eBird data statistical modeling that accounts for variation in observer effort is required. While eBird alone is not ideal for rigorous effects-of-management occupancy analysis it can supplement structured surveys. Search for observations from your site on eBird Explore. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, additional tools and resources here, and see how eBird can be used for effects monitoring here.",L-EO-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LEA,,"eBird: eBird checklists from your site can provide detection counts but because observer effort and distribution vary widely eBird data are not well suited as the primary source for effects-of-management relative abundance analysis. Consider using eBird as a supplement to structured point counts or transects which provide more controlled and comparable data. Search for observations from your site on eBird Explore. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, additional tools and resources here, and see how eBird can be used for effects monitoring here.",L-EA-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LSR,,"eBird: eBird checklists from your site or nearby areas provide an accessible species list for a richness snapshot. Search your location in eBird Explore to see recent detections. Coverage depends on where birders visit so some areas of your site may be underrepresented. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SR-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LSO,,"eBird: eBird checklists from your site or nearby areas can indicate which species have been detected and provide presence/absence data for a snapshot of occupancy. For formal occupancy estimation from eBird data statistical modeling that accounts for variation in observer effort is required. Search your location in eBird Explore or submit your own checklists. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SO-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LSA,,"eBird: eBird Status and Trends provides modeled relative abundance maps accessible through eBird Status and Trends. These products give a snapshot of relative abundance at approximately 3km resolution; they are modeled estimates and model accuracy may be limited at fine local scales. For site-specific data submit your own eBird checklists to add to the local record. Search for observations from your site on eBird Explore. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-SA-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LTR,,"eBird: eBird trend data from eBird Status and Trends can provide short-term (10-year) trend context at regional scales. For local-scale trend monitoring structured fixed-location surveys are more appropriate than eBird alone because eBird observer effort and coverage change over time in ways that can obscure real trends at a single site. eBird is best used as a complement to structured monitoring. eBird Status and Trends trend data are available at 27x27km resolution and are most suitable for regional rather than local-scale trend monitoring; consider pairing with local survey data for finer-scale assessments. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TR-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LTO,,"eBird: eBird trend data from eBird Status and Trends can provide regional-scale occupancy or occurrence trend context. For local-scale occupancy trends structured fixed-location surveys with repeated visits are more appropriate. eBird can serve as useful supplementary context for local trends you observe. eBird Status and Trends trend data are available at 27x27km resolution and are most suitable for regional rather than local-scale trend monitoring; consider pairing with local survey data for finer-scale assessments. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TO-V-EB EndPoint,ebird_LTA,,"eBird: eBird trend data from eBird Status and Trends can provide short-term relative abundance trend context at regional scales. For local-scale abundance trends structured fixed-location counts are more reliable because eBird effort and coverage change over time. eBird is best used as supplementary context for your local monitoring program. eBird Status and Trends trend data are available at 27x27km resolution and are most suitable for regional rather than local-scale trend monitoring; consider pairing with local survey data for finer-scale assessments. Learn more about monitoring with eBird here, see customized instruction protocols here, and additional tools and resources here.",L-TA-V-EB EndPoint,fixed_vol_L,,"Fixed Location Counts (Volunteer): Volunteers can conduct fixed location counts by returning to the same vantage point and recording all birds within view or earshot during a set time period. This approach is especially accessible for monitoring waterbirds, migrating raptors, colonial nesters, and other species detectable from a distance from an open vantage point. Standardized datasheets and a simple protocol (e.g. a 10-minute count at the same time of year) allow volunteers to generate reliable data. Training volunteers to record effort information (start time, location, weather) is important for data quality. See the Cornell Bird Monitoring Toolkit for volunteer-friendly protocols. Learn more about hawk counting and see example protocols at HawkWatch International.",L-V-FL

name: source_docs/MonitoringToolReview_Danielle_July2026.csv
content:
Text Code,Notes
Q-1,"delete ""return to previous question and"" since it is displayed on the same page"
SN-R-2,"I think there needs to be some sort of brief explanation or link to what the ebird status and trends dataset is here, unless you want to save those portions for resources. Either way, I think either the SN-R-2 or SN-R-5 could use a small explanation describing status and trends, much like the pop-up hover for the ebird resrouces and bba resources in SN-O-10 and SN-O-12. You could even use the same hover text for SN-O-10."
SN-R-5,should some of the information in SN-O-11 also be copied over to SN-R-5?
SN-A-9,should SN-A-9 be made consistent with SN-O-10?
SN-A-10,"should SN-A-10 be made more consistent with SN-O-11? They have links to different pages and descriptions that I think could be helpful for both sections. I understand that one is occupancy, and one is relative abundance, so there has to be some difference."
TR-A-1,"I would say choose the population size question ""at the level above"""
TR-R-2,"I think there needs to be some sort of brief explanation or link to what the ebird status and trends dataset is here. Either way, I think either this could use a small explanation describing status and trends, much like the pop-up hover for the ebird resrouces and bba resources in SN-O-10 and SN-O-12. You could even use the same hover text for SN-O-10. Also, the link in the eBird Trends Data product guidance page does not go to the top of the page, but to the mulit-species section. I am sure this was done on purpose but just want to double check."
TR-O-10,SN-O-10 and TR-O-10 should be made consistent
TR-O-12,should be made consistent with SN-O-12. either combine or choose the one you like more. I like SN-O-12 more.
TR-A-9,make consistent with SN-A-9 and SN-O-10
PS-2,"make more consistent with SN-O-12, but keep the sentence about point counts"
L-ER-T-PC,"link can be more specific to point count rather than to top of page, and just make hyperlinks for the word ""here"" for consistency with other methods; discrepency in language between accounting for imperfect detection with L-EO-T-PC, L-EA-T-PC (sometimes switching between multiple observers, distance bands/minutes of observation, and repeated visits); in general make sure consistency is there for imperfect detections for point counts and change all the hyperlinks to just ""here"""
OB-3,"this text is also visible during the volunteer observer selection, when acoustics are not mentioned. I would remove from volunteer section to eliminate confusion"
L-EO-T-PC,"link can be more specific to point count rather than to top of page, and just make hyperlinks for the word ""here"" for consistency with toher methods"
L-V-FL,"this can apply to all fixed location count volunteer and technical sections, but do we want to include a link to hawkwatch international for examples? They have a good protocols page https://www.hawkmigration.org/data-submission/; also I know you said not to worry about types but all volunteer fixed location counts need commas in (start time location weather)"
L-ER-V-EB,may also want to include ebird explore link
L-EO-V-EB,may also want to include ebird explore link
L-EA-V-EB,may also want to include ebird explore link
L-SA-V-EB,"because we mentioned status and trends so much on the regional scale, I would include the finest scale at which you can get data for ebird status and trends so people know what they are working with. May want to add ebird explore link. Also, in trends sections for relative abundance for volunteers, you say status and trends is for regional scale and not reliable for local, with the suggestion to pair it with other methods. Does that also apply here? May want to make that language consistent."
L-TR-V-EB,maybe include the finest scale at which you can get data for ebird status and trends so people know what they are working with
L-TO-V-EB,maybe include the finest scale at which you can get data for ebird status and trends so people know what they are working with
L-TA-T-AR,"add this sentence in before ""Consistent deployment"" sentence: Acoustic detection rates from automated classifiers provide an index of relative abundance."
L-TA-V-EB,maybe include the finest scale at which you can get data for ebird status and trends so people know what they are working with
General,some of the pop-up hover boxes are white while others are black. May want to standardize
General,"A back button may also be helpful in addition to the reset button, or maybe instead of a back button, a header that is a table of contents that links to each page? It can be a bit difficult/tedious to remember the path you were just on to choose an alternate choice, especially on the local scale when you might want to explore options between technical and volunteer observers"
General,"I think a header page (with intro, tools, cost comparison) that also has all links included in the tool organized by resource would be helpful. For example, there are a variety of ebird status and trends links spread thorughout and someone may just want all the status and trends resources all together without having to fish through the whole tool."
General,"I think hover texts for regional resources (BBS, BBA, ebird, etc) should be consistent for each resource across all question types"

- Seeing what the options are, faciliting the discussion\

- Researching - new students, instruction in undergrad ecology\

- Labs, community groups coming out to lands\
- Interns\

	- Interns come out and work on the farm\
- Early career biologists in state agencies\
- Organization applying for grants - costs\
\
Accessibility:\
- Links and minimal text is good. \
Probably users don\'92t want all the extra information\
But it would be good to pu\
Video of how it works (eg. ARUs)\
Visuals - little icons, symbols\
\
2. Impediments\
- Time and bandwidth limitations to know what\'92s out there and available\
- Being aware of tradeoffs\
- Having resources and time, technical skills (in terms of data collection)\
- Longevity of projects\
- Network of people with the technical abilities: - list of people with expertise, or listserv google group\
	- Question forum\
- Project examples (design to analysis) - on the tool\
\
3. \
- Cost comparison is the unique thing - novel\
(DNR - batteries for ARUs - having own battery box on tool.  Rechargeable.)\
Break out batteries and refurbishment/replacement (10% audiomoth replacement)\
\
- Labs coming in with students\
\
Estimating number of points - power analysis?\
\
Merlin\
\
Caution - manager gungho about their property - eager to point counts, but eBird may answer\
\
Local vs. regional - say up front about end points\
\

name: source_docs/UpdatingShinyLive.txt
content:
If you're changing text content only (labels, descriptions, resource links):

1. Edit DecisionToolText.csv directly
2. Skip to step 3 below

If you're changing the app code/structure:

1. Edit app.R in RStudio
2. Test it locally by running the app normally in RStudio (just click Run App)

Then for both:

3. In R, re-export the Shinylive site:
setwd("C:/Users/ehunter1/OneDrive - Virginia Tech/2025/AMJVMonitoring")
shinylive::export(
  appdir  = ".",
  destdir = "site",
  appFiles = c("app.R", "DecisionToolText.csv", "www/amjv.jpg")
)
3b. Open the site/ folder in the AMJVMonitoring folder. Copy all contents and then paste (rewrite) into the Documents/GitHub/amjv-monitoring-tool folder.
4. Open GitHub Desktop, which will show the changed files in the site/ folder
5. Write a short description of the change in the bottom-left box (e.g. "Updated occupancy text")
6. Click Commit to main
7. Click Push origin
8. Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub Pages to update, then visit your site

If you don't see your changes in the browser: hard refresh with Ctrl+Shift+R, or open DevTools (F12) → Application → Service Workers → Unregister → Clear site data → Ctrl+Shift+R


###
To turn off review codes for production, just change REVIEW_MODE <- TRUE to REVIEW_MODE <- FALSE in app.R — no other changes needed.

These checklists are reviewed by automated filters and trained ebird moderators to flag any unusual or potentially incorrect submissions. eBird Status and Trends scientists combine raw eBird data, satellite imagery, statistical models, and machine learning to predict population trends and occurrence across space and time. These population and occurrence predictions are then built into visualizations and summary statistics designed for professional use.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="0000003F"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading4"/><w:rPr><w:highlight w:val="yellow"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:bookmarkStart w:colFirst="0" w:colLast="0" w:name="_yuohjknsp79h" w:id="24"/><w:bookmarkEnd w:id="24"/><w:commentRangeStart w:id="15"/><w:commentRangeStart w:id="16"/><w:commentRangeStart w:id="17"/><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Resources: eBird</w:t></w:r><w:commentRangeEnd w:id="15"/><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:commentReference w:id="15"/></w:r><w:commentRangeEnd w:id="16"/><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:commentReference w:id="16"/></w:r><w:commentRangeEnd w:id="17"/><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:commentReference w:id="17"/></w:r><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000040"><w:pPr><w:rPr/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Check out <a href='https://science.ebird.org/en/status-and-trends' target='_blank'>eBird Status and Trends</a> and type in your species of interest. Maps are predictions of relative abundance (occupancy can be inferred by any pixel that is colored in, and areas in gray are where the species in inferred to be absent). You can get regional estimates using drop down menus (country/state, and ultimately other regions like JVs) or drawing a polygon. The maps may provide more nuanced information than these estimates, especially if your state covers different ecoregions where trends may differ. If you have some R experience, you can follow <a href='https://ebird.github.io/ebird-best-practices/ ' target='_blank'>tutorials</a> to get encounter rate, which is proportional to occupancy. You can also download raw eBird data from <a href='https://www.gbif.org/dataset/4fa7b334-ce0d-4e88-aaae-2e0c138d049e ' target='_blank'>GBIF</a>. If you think the eBird estimates are incomplete and you have survey data to share with eBird, you can do so using <a href='https://support.ebird.org/en/support/solutions/articles/48000907878-upload-spreadsheet-data-to-ebird ' target='_blank'>bulk uploads</a>. There are options to hide locations for private lands.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000041"><w:pPr><w:rPr/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000042"><w:pPr><w:rPr/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Hover text: BBA</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000043"><w:pPr><w:rPr/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">BBA surveys are population surveys conducted at the regional (typically state/provincial) level. Each atlas divides its survey area into grids (blocks) and assigns volunteers to a specific block. The volunteers thoroughly survey their block. Overall coverage in a block may be limited by accessibility issues such as private land access. Volunteers are specifically looking for signs of breeding activity, with any evidence categorized as “confirmed”, “probable”, or “possible”. Data from recent atlases are collected in the form of checklists for each site visited in a block, often through eBird. Older atlases often collected data cumulatively over a breeding season with only the highest breeding status noted, and limited, if any, date information. </w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000044"><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading4"/><w:rPr><w:highlight w:val="yellow"/></w:rPr></w:pPr><w:bookmarkStart w:colFirst="0" w:colLast="0" w:name="_rdsh0y4lu3q5" w:id="25"/><w:bookmarkEnd w:id="25"/><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Resources: BBA</w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr></w:r></w:p><w:p w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidP="00000000" w:rsidRDefault="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000" w14:paraId="00000045"><w:pPr><w:rPr/></w:pPr><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">BBA resources vary state by state, but can include: maps, raw data, and timing of BBA surveys. Given how most BBAs are conducted, estimates of occupancy are typically available for most breeding species in recent atlases. Most BBAs were typically published as books (e.g., <a href='https://www.psupress.org/books/titles/978-0-271-08980-5.html' target='_blank'>West Virginia 2nd BBA</a>), and more recently are being published as interactive websites (e.g., <a href='https://mnbirdatlas.org/' target='_blank'>Minnesota BBA</a>). At each stop, the observer records all birds seen or heard during a 3-minute count period, following standardized protocols to maximize consistency among routes and years. Most routes are surveyed once annually by trained volunteers, often by the same observer across years, which helps maintain consistency in detection ability. w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">The North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) is a long-term, standardized monitoring program in which skilled observers conduct roadside bird counts along fixed routes during the peak of the breeding season (typically May–June). Each route is about 39.4 km (24.5 miles) long and consists of 50 stops spaced 0.8 km (0.5 miles) apart. At each stop, the observer records all birds seen or heard during a 3-minute count period, following standardized protocols to maximize consistency among routes and years. Most routes are surveyed once annually by trained volunteers, often by the same observer across years, which helps maintain consistency in detection ability. For </w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:u w:val="single"/><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">trends in relative abundance</w:t></w:r><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">, use the USGS analyzed BBS results (</w:t></w:r><w:hyperlink r:id="rId23"><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:color w:val="1155cc"/><w:u w:val="single"/><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">https://eesc.usgs.gov/mbr/bbs2024/index.html</w:t></w:r></w:hyperlink><w:r w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">). points on the landscape to record bird vocalizations on a preset schedule. The recording schedule is highly dependent upon your study objectives and scale of interest. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Transect surveys consist of a trained observer walking along a specified route and recording all the birds seen and heard within a fixed time frame and typically within a fixed distance out from the transect line. If the distribution and habitat selection of only a single species or a subset of focal species is of interest, transects can still be valuable. The trained observers only need to know how to identify the focal species of interest. Observed birds can be assigned to distance bands and/or the segments of the transect in which they are observed so that detection probability can be determined. Transect routes are often distributed across habitat types or along environmental gradients within the focal site. This is still important even if focused on a single/few species because it is impossible to determine habitat associations without sampling a wide range of habitats and environmental characteristics. Occupancy (species presence) can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected along transect routes, or more broadly to features collected across clusters of routes, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Acoustics description: Acoustic surveys consist of trained personnel placing acoustic recording units (ARUs) at fixed points on the landscape to record bird vocalizations on a preset schedule. The recording schedule is highly dependent upon your study objectives and scale of interest. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. If the distribution and habitat selection of only a single species or a subset of focal species is of interest, acoustics can still be valuable. The processing pipeline can be restricted to the focal species of interest. ARU points are often distributed across a variety of habitat types and environmental characteristics. This is still important even if focused on a single/few species because it is impossible to determine habitat associations without sampling a wide range of habitats and environmental characteristics. Occupancy (species presence in a recording) can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected at the deployment points, or more broadly to features collected across a cluster of points, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. Initial financial input for this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. If the relative abundance of only a single species or a subset of focal species is of interest, transects can still be valuable. The trained observers only need to know how to identify the focal species of interest. Observed birds can be assigned to distance bands and/or the segments of the transect in which they are observed so that detection probability can be determined. Transect routes are often distributed across habitat types or along environmental gradients within the focal site. This is still important even if focused on a single/few species because it is impossible to determine relative abundance without sampling a wide range of habitats and environmental characteristics. Relative abundance can be assessed as a function of habitat features (i.e. disturbance event, restoration efforts) also collected along transect routes, or more broadly to features collected across clusters of routes, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. the birds seen and heard within a fixed time frame and typically within a fixed distance out from the transect line. Observed birds can be assigned to distance bands and/or the segments of the transect in which they are observed so that detection probability can be determined. Transect routes are often distributed across habitat types or along environmental gradients within the focal site. If the number (richness) and composition of only a subset of focal species is of interest, transects can still be valuable. The trained observers only need to know how to identify the focal species of interest. The number of observed species (richness) can be assessed as a function of habitat features also collected along transect routes, or more broadly to features collected across clusters of routes, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Acoustics description: Acoustic surveys consist of trained personnel placing acoustic recording units (ARUs) at fixed points on the landscape to record bird vocalizations on a preset schedule. The recording schedule is highly dependent upon your study objectives and scale of interest. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species.  If the number and composition or a subset of focal species is of interest, acoustics can still be valuable. The processing pipeline can be restricted to the focal species of interest. ARU points are often distributed across a variety of habitat types and environmental characteristics. This is still important even if focused on a single/few species because it is impossible to determine habitat associations without sampling a wide range of habitats and environmental characteristics.The number of species (richness) can be assessed as a function of habitat features also collected at the deployment points, or more broadly to features collected across a cluster of points, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. Initial financial investments in this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you. and typically within a fixed distance out from the transect line. If the true abundance of only a single species is of interest, transects can still be valuable. The trained observers only need to know how to identify the focal species of interest. Observed birds can be assigned to distance bands and/or the segments of the transect in which they are observed so that detection probability can be determined. Transect routes are often distributed across habitat types or along environmental gradients within the focal site. This is still important even if focused on a single species because it is impossible to determine true abundance without sampling a wide range of habitats and environmental characteristics. True abundance can be assessed as a function of habitat features also collected along transect routes, or more broadly to features collected across clusters of routes, depending on your objectives and scale of interest. w:rsidDel="00000000" w:rsidR="00000000" w:rsidRPr="00000000"><w:rPr><w:rtl w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Acoustics description: Acoustic surveys consist of trained personnel placing acoustic recording units (ARUs) at fixed points on the landscape to record bird vocalizations on a preset schedule. The recording schedule is highly dependent upon your study objectives and scale of interest. Once the devices are collected from the landscape, the recordings are processed through automated and/or manual pipelines to detect, identify, and verify the vocalizing species. The number (richness) and composition of species can be tracked over your desired time interval through multiple ARU deployments. ARUs are well-suited for repeated data collection because recorder settings can be standardized across deployments and devices. Initial financial input for this method can be high but worth the investment, particularly for long-term projects or organizations with limited available man-power. Please see the cost comparison tool to help determine if ARUs are right for you.
